Estimators, one or more: Two-Way Fixed Effects and Sun and Abraham: the regression on leads and lags of the first treatment with unit and time effects, and Sun and Abraham's (2021) estimator, which stays right when the effects differ between cohorts; Callaway and Sant'Anna: their (2021) effect of each cohort at each time, against the Control units (Never Treated, Not Yet Treated, Treated Last, or Auto, the never treated when there are any), by a Method (Doubly Robust, Inverse Probability Weighting, Outcome Regression), and its averages; Stepped Wedge: the mixed model of Hussey and Hughes (2007) for a trial whose clusters cross to treatment one group after another, with an Effect (Immediate Treatment, one effect; Exposure Time Indicators, one for each time since the cross; or Heterogeneity by Exposure Time), averaged over exposure times From to To or taken At one, and an Outcome Type, continuous or binary (0 or 1, or successes out of Trials). It needs a treatment indicator. Event Times: the Leads before the first treatment, for the test of pre-trends, and the Lags after it. Then Make Study.

Your Studies shows the table, its columns and the estimators. Open Notebook opens study.ipynb, which installs EventStudies.jl from the Pollis registry (and MixedModels.jl for the stepped wedge), runs the estimators study.toml names on panel.csv and writes the results to results/. The page then draws: each estimator's effects by event time with their 95% intervals, 0 being the first time treated (the stepped wedge's exposure time 1), and a table of them; the tests of pre-trends: an F test of the effects before treatment; Callaway and Sant'Anna's averages: simple, over event times, over cohorts and over calendar times; the stepped wedge's estimate, with the intracluster correlation. The page redraws when results/ changes: after an edit of study.toml, run the notebook again. Which estimator Two-way fixed effects averages the effects with weights that can be negative when the effects grow over time, because units treated earlier serve as controls for those treated later. Sun and Abraham, and Callaway and Sant'Anna, compare each cohort only with units not yet or never treated; when they agree with each other and not with two-way fixed effects, trust them. Units treated from the first time have no time before treatment to compare with, and the estimators leave them out. No results yet & A panel study: open its notebook and run it. Pre-trends: not tested & Callaway and Sant'Anna's test takes every cohort's effect at every time before treatment; with more of them than units, as with many cohorts over many years, it cannot be made. Their effects by event time before 0 still show any pre-trend. Not a table & The file needs a header row and three columns or more, separated by commas. The stepped wedge needs a treatment indicator & Under Treated, choose Treatment Indicator and a column that is not 0 from the time a unit is treated.

Finding out how fast your Julia code is and why, and checking that its results are right. Two menus of Compose look at code rather than data. Profiling measures how long code takes and finds the cause, in the order of the work: measure, find the cause and fix it, then compare versions of a package and languages. Each entry is a panel, whose tabs are the ways of doing the task (Inside a Panel, page ).

Entry Tabs What it tells you Time a Function... Chairmarks, BenchmarkTools, First Call The time and the allocations of a call, from many samples, and the first call, compiling included Find Where the Time Goes... Flame Graph, Line by Line, Text Report The functions and the lines the time goes to, from Julia's profiler Time Sections of Code... Labelled Sections, Every Statement, Test Sets The calls, the time and the allocations of each part of a script you mark, in one table

Entry Tabs What it tells you Find Allocations... By Line, By Type, Possible Allocations Where the code takes memory on the heap, and what a function could allocate Check Type Stability... Inferred Types, Runtime Dispatches, Stability Check Whether Julia can infer one concrete type for each result and variable Speed Up a Function... The Function, Diagnose, Change, Compare A function from slow to fast in four steps, the two versions checked to give the same result In the Change step of Speed Up a Function, Speed Up with Agent hands the change to your coding agent, which explains its plan before it writes the faster version (Orchestration, page ).

Entry Tabs What it tells you Compare Package Versions... Releases, Local Clone The same code timed with several versions of a package, each in a new Julia Load and Compile Time... Load Time, First Use, Inference Time The wait before the first result: loading the packages, compiling and inference

Entry Tabs What it tells you Run a Speed Race... Loop, Vectorised, Sort The same computation in Julia, Python and R, on the same data, each timed in its own language Add a Language... C, Fortran, Rust The race in a compiled language, built with the compiler on your computer and called from Julia Add a Language joins the race of Run a Speed Race when that race ran in the session on the same values; otherwise it races Julia alone. Fortran, with no sort in its standard library, runs Loop and Vectorised. A time belongs to its computer A time depends on the computer, on what else it runs, and on the versions of Julia and the packages. Compare times taken on the same computer, in the same session, and read a speed race as a result about that race, not about the languages. Fast code is worth having only when its results are right. Correctness Tests checks them in two ways: against values that someone else has certified, and against rules the results must obey.

Compose > Correctness Tests > Published Benchmarks lists problems whose results have been certified by their publisher. Click a name to open your own copy of its notebook, made in ~/.pollis/correctness the first time; the notebook checks Julia's results against the certified ones. NIST StRD, the Statistical Reference Datasets of the National Institute of Standards and Technology: univariate summary statistics, one-way analysis of variance, linear regression and nonlinear regression. GARCH(1,1): the benchmark of Fiorentini, Calzolari and Panattoni. Compare with Saved Results... keeps your own results as known values: once a result is right, the ReferenceTests package saves it as a reference file, in ~/.pollis/reference-tests, and each later run fails if the result has changed. Its tabs save Numbers in full, compared within a tolerance, Printed Output as you read it, a Plot as an image, or only a Hash. The first run saves the reference; run the code again to compare.

Check a Property... tries a property, a rule that must hold for every input, on inputs that the Supposition package generates. When an input breaks the rule, Supposition shrinks it to the smallest input that still does, and prints it. Choose a tab: Invariant, a rule true of every result, such as a variance that is never negative; Round Trip, a function followed by its inverse giving back the input; or Simple Version, a fast function against a simple one taken as right. Set Examples, the most inputs tried, and Seed: the same seed tries the same inputs again. Run the code. Test passed means that no input tried broke the rule; Found counterexample gives the input that did. Simple Version ends on a counterexample: for [999000.0, 999000.01], a variance computed in one pass gives 0.0 where var gives 5.0e-5, as subtracting two large sums loses the digits of a small difference. Welford's Algorithm, in its Next Steps, checks a one-pass variance without that subtraction. Check a Convergence Order... tests a solver of a differential equation by the rate at which its error falls: a solver of order p divides its error by about 2^(p) when its step is halved. Its tabs estimate the order of an ODE Solver, and the SDE Strong Order and SDE Weak Order of a stochastic one; @test passes when the estimate lies within the Allowed Gap of the theory. A pass is not a proof A benchmark that passes says that Julia's results are right on its problems, and a property that passes, that the rule held on the inputs tried. Neither says that the code is right on every input; a failure, by contrast, gives an input you can run again. No GCC found & In Add a Language, install GCC: on macOS with Homebrew (brew install gcc), which also installs gfortran. No rustc found & Install Rust with rustup, from rustup.rs. … the two programs do not compute the same thing & The language's result differs from Julia's, and the race is not timed until they agree. Set Local Clone to the folder of a clone & In Compare Package Versions, give the folder of a clone of the package, such as one made by Pkg.develop in ~/.julia/dev.

Julia code taken beyond Julia: into a library, a program, a web page, another language or a database, and checked against Julia each time. Compilation Lab compiles a Julia function for use outside Julia, or calls compiled code from Julia. Every entry has the same example: the number of iterations at each pixel of the Mandelbrot set or of the Julia set of c. Each one checks that the count at every pixel is Julia's before it times anything, so a faster version is known to compute the same thing. Programs and libraries go in the programs folder of the open Pollis Workspace (page ); Choose..., beside Folder, picks another.

Entry Tabs or steps What you get Compile Julia to a Shared Library... JuliaC, PackageCompiler, StaticCompiler A library that a C program calls, checked against Julia; Python and R call the same library in Next Steps Compile Julia to an Executable... JuliaC, PackageCompiler, StaticCompiler A program that draws the picture by itself, from a terminal or a double-click, timed against julia running the same script Compile Julia to WebAssembly... The Function, Compile, Check, Live View A module that runs in the page, checked against Julia, then drawing the set live as you zoom with the mouse wheel and drag

Entry Tabs or steps What you get Mix Julia with Compiled Code... Call C, Call Fortran, Call C++, Julia Callback, Julia from C Julia calling compiled code with @ccall, a compiled loop calling back into Julia, and a C program calling Julia Translate Julia to Rust... The Function, Translate, Build, Compare The function written in Rust, built with cargo and called from Julia; Translate with Agent hands your own function to your coding agent Julia Functions in DuckDB... Julia Function, Rust Extension The function inside SQL queries: registered from the Julia session, or compiled into a DuckDB extension

section: Three tools for libraries and programs
text: The tabs of Shared Library and Executable are three ways to compile the same Julia code. JuliaC, the default, needs Julia 1.12 or later; it trims the result to the code it reaches, which keeps it small and quick to start, but it refuses calls it cannot resolve when it compiles. PackageCompiler keeps the whole Julia runtime, so anything that runs in a session runs, in a much larger folder. StaticCompiler writes a single file with no Julia runtime, as a C compiler would, for code that never needs Julia's garbage collector. Sizes and Build Times and Start-Up and Run Time (Start-Up and Call Time for a library) set the tools side by side.

Through Rust translates the function to Rust and builds it with cargo. Through C translates it to C and builds it with clang and wasm-ld, which come as Julia packages, so nothing else is installed. With WebAssemblyCompiler.jl compiles the Julia function itself, in a Julia 1.10 that the code starts through juliaup. In Next Steps, The Same in JavaScript times the function written in JavaScript beside each module, and Compare the Ways sets the three modules side by side: what each needs, its size, its fastest time, its calls into WebAssembly and the pixels where its counts differ, expected to be none.

Julia Sets Along a Circle (Executable): a program draws the Julia set of c as c turns round a circle, frame after frame, shown as an animated picture. Use All the Cores and Write a PNG with a Package (Executable, JuliaC and PackageCompiler): the program on several threads, and a program that uses a Julia package. Options with Names (Executable): a command line such as --width 800, in any order. Call the Library from Python and Call the Library from R (Shared Library). Fused and Not Fused (Mix): the compiled code built again so that it fuses a multiplication and an addition, and the pixels whose count then differs from Julia's. Query Plan and Query Times (Julia Functions in DuckDB). The same answer, pixel by pixel Every entry compares whole numbers, the count at each pixel, rather than pictures that look alike. Near the edge of the set a different last bit in one multiplication changes a count, so the compiled code performs Julia's operations in the same order and never fuses a multiplication and an addition, which Julia does not do unless asked.

A C compiler, for Mix, the calling program of Shared Library and the JuliaC and PackageCompiler tabs of Executable: the Command Line Tools on macOS (xcode-select --install), gcc on Linux, MinGW-w64 on Windows; and gfortran for Call Fortran. Rust, with cargo, from rustup.rs, for Translate Julia to Rust, the Rust Extension of Julia Functions in DuckDB and WebAssembly Through Rust. Julia 1.10 through juliaup (juliaup add 1.10) for WebAssembly With WebAssemblyCompiler.jl. Python 3 and R, only for the Next Steps that call the library from them. An entry asks to install the Julia packages it needs when it opens; the code of the JuliaC tabs installs JuliaC itself the first time it runs.

Working with others at their own computers: a chat, sharing code, datasets, files and databases, and editing files together. A session connects up to five people, each at their own copy of Pollis: two colleagues, a student and a tutor, or a small team. In a Side by Side session everyone keeps their own editors and notebooks; in the chat you talk, and you share what you choose, when you choose. In a Same Page session everyone edits the files of one folder of the host's together (Edit together, below). Nobody can run anything on anyone else's computer.

Pollis on each computer, and an Internet connection. A network that lets sessions through. To check, choose Compose > Collaboration > Test Connection... before the session, and send its results (Copy Results) if you need help.

Choose Compose > Collaboration > Start Side by Side Session... Type your name, as the others will see it. The chat opens beside your editor, and the invitation is copied to the clipboard. Paste the invitation into an email or a message to the others. To copy it again, use Copy Invitation at the top of the chat, or Compose > Collaboration > Invite People... You are the host: you admit the others, up to five in all, and when you leave the session ends for everyone.

Choose Compose > Collaboration > Join Session... Paste the invitation you received, or type its code: four groups of five letters and digits, such as 7KQ2M-.... Type your name. The chat opens and says when you have joined.

Write a message and press Enter; Shift+Enter starts a new line. Paste or drag an image into the message: larger images are reduced to fit the limit of 2 MB. The + button in the message box adds: Image: a PNG, JPEG, GIF or WebP image, shown in the chat. File: any file up to 5 MB. The others get a card with Save As...; Pollis never opens or runs it. Dragging a file that is not an image into the chat shares it the same way. Dataset: a CSV file up to 5 MB (see the next page). Database: a DuckDB database up to 5 MB (see the next page). Show Participants lists who is in the session and whether each connection is direct or through a relay.

The host chooses Compose > Collaboration > Start Same Page Session..., picks the folder to share, one of the workspace's or another (Choose a Folder...), and confirms. The others join as for any session. Beside the messages, the chat lists the files of the folder. Click one to open it: the host gets their own file, and the others get it in their own window, beside their own folder. Type as usual. The others' changes appear as they make them, and each person's cursor shows in a colour, with their name. Undo undoes only your own changes. Save, on any computer, writes the file to the host's disk. The others can edit text files of up to 2 MB, but not create, rename or delete files, and each runs code in their own Julia session. Notebooks are not edited together yet: share them with Share My Editor.

Any participant can choose Compose > Collaboration > Invite an Agent...: a coding agent of Model Tasks and Routing (Claude Code, Codex or OpenCode, on a cloud or a local model) joins under the name they give it, shown as Gemma (invited by Ana). Anyone asks it something by starting a message with @Gemma: it answers in the chat, and a file it writes reaches everyone as a snapshot, with Compare with Mine. It runs on the inviter's computer, at their cost (nothing on a local model), reads only the chat and what was shared, in a folder of its own deleted when it leaves, and cannot open other files or reach the Internet. Invite an Agent... again removes it. The invitation is the key Anyone with the invitation can join while the session lasts, and receives whatever is shared from then on. Send it only to the people you mean, and do not share personal or confidential data in a session whose invitation may have gone further.

While you are in a session, a bar at the bottom of each editor and notebook shows Share My Editor. It sends a snapshot of what you see, unsaved changes included; a notebook is sent without its outputs. For a Pluto notebook in Pollis's browser, use the Share My Editor button in the browser's toolbar. Sharing again replaces the earlier snapshot. Code files and notebooks up to 2 MB can be shared. The others see your snapshot read-only, with two buttons below it: Compare with Mine: your snapshot and their own editor side by side, line by line. Copy to My Editor: replaces the content of their own editor, or the cells of their own notebook, with yours. Undo brings theirs back, except in Pluto.

A dataset (CSV): + > Dataset in the chat, Share Dataset on a CSV file in the Explorer, or Share Dataset in the toolbar of a Julia table viewer. Pollis asks before sending. The others get a card with the first five rows and Preview, Save to My Workspace and Load into My Julia Session, which reads it into a Julia table named after the file. A database (DuckDB): + > Database. Pollis asks before sending the whole database. The others get a card with Save As... and Attach in My Julia Session, which opens it read-only, as a variable named after the file, and shows its tables in the Databases view. Before sharing a database Changes made in a Julia session that still has the database open may not be in the file yet: close that connection, or run CHECKPOINT, before sharing. And attach only databases from people you trust: a database can hold views that read files on the computer where they are queried.

In Compose > Collaboration > Session Settings... the host ticks Lock the Session so that nobody else can join, even with the invitation; someone whose connection dropped can still come back. In a Same Page session, everyone can edit on joining: the host unticks a participant to let them only watch, with the files read-only for them while they still see every change. The chat says each change and marks the watchers.

The tutor starts one with Compose > Classroom > Start Class Session...; up to 30 students join with Join Session..., each connected to the tutor only, who passes on what they write and share. Show to the Class shows a student's snapshot to the others; Class Chat, in Session Settings..., lets everyone see every message. Split into Breakout Groups... makes groups at random, which the tutor can change; the tutor sees them all, speaks to one with Visit a Group..., and ends them with Bring Everyone Back.

Leave Session, at the top of the chat or in Compose > Collaboration, leaves the session. When the host leaves, the session ends for everyone. If the host's connection drops, the others wait a minute for it to come back. After the session the chat stays open, to be read, until you close it. The host's files open in a Same Page session can then no longer be saved: Save As... keeps a copy.

Free public servers introduce the participants to each other; after that each pair connects directly. The servers never see the session code or anything you share. By default they are nostr relays; on networks that block those, set pollis.collaboration.signalling to mqtt before starting the session (the invitation tells the others). A relay for networks that block direct connections is not set up yet. ``Could not reach the session" & Check the code, and that the host is still in the session. Then run Test Connection... on both computers. Test Connection: no introduction server reachable & The network blocks Pollis (often a firewall or proxy): try another network, such as a phone's hotspot. Test Connection: nostr blocked, MQTT reachable & The host sets pollis.collaboration.signalling to mqtt and starts a new session. Two people never connect & Both networks may block direct connections: one of them tries another network. ``The session is full" & A session has at most five participants, the host included. ``... has locked the session" & Ask the host to untick Lock the Session in Session Settings..., then join again. A file, dataset or database is refused & It is over 5 MB, or not what it says it is: send it the usual way.

Choosing and starting coding agents, and routing tasks to models. Some tasks of the Compose menu are done by a coding agent, a program that writes code and documents in a terminal: creating panels, packaging toolboxes, writing methods and vignettes, polishing reports. Their menu items carry a sparkle, because they run on your agent's account and cost tokens. Pollis works with any agent: you choose which, and which model each task runs on.

Choose Compose > Coding Agents. The page lists Claude Code, Codex and OpenCode, each with its command and whether it is On This Computer: Agent Installed, or Install Agent, which opens its install page. Click Install Skills, so that the agents know the Pollis skills in any folder, even outside Pollis. Later, Update installs their latest version. Under Other Agents, Add an Agent adds an agent of your own: a name, such as MyAgent, and its command line, with {prompt} where the first message goes; without it, Pollis copies the message to the clipboard, to paste into the agent. Which agent runs a task is chosen in Model Tasks and Routing.

section: What happens when a task starts
text: Pollis opens a terminal, starts the agent of the task's tier there, on the tier's model, and gives it a first message that points it to the skill for the task. From then on you talk to the agent in that terminal.

A skill is the know-how an agent reads to do a task. Compose > Agent Skills lists them, downloaded in their latest version when the page opens: create-panel, explain-differences, package-toolbox, plan-replication, polish-report, prepare-method, references, replicate-article, tables-from-article, write-method and write-vignette, each with its Tasks and Example Requests. View Skill opens it; Run with My Agent starts it on the Standard tier.

Not every task needs the strongest model. Compose > Orchestration > Model Tasks and Routing has three tiers, and any of your own, such as Max: Light: small tasks, on a fast, cheap or local model. Standard: everyday tasks. Strong: hard tasks, where a mistake costs most. A tier is a cell of a table, whose columns are the Code Agents, Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and your own, and whose rows are the Models: Cloud, such as Claude Haiku 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-5.5 or Gemini 4 Argon, and Local, the chat models on this computer. Type a tier's name in a cell, and the tier is that agent on that model; a new name makes a new tier. A tier is in one cell only, and a dash marks a model the agent cannot run. Unless you change them, Light, Standard and Strong are Claude Code on Haiku, Sonnet and Opus. Below it, Tasks gives each task its tier, under Runs On, and the skills it reads, under Skills: Task Menu Runs On Skills Polish with Agent Reports Light polish-report Write a Vignette Replication Standard write-vignette Prepare for Registration Replication Standard prepare-method Package a Toolbox Compose Standard package-toolbox Tables from the Article Replication Strong tables-from-article Write a Method Replication Strong write-method Plan a Replication Replication Standard plan-replication Replicate an Article Replication Strong replicate-article Explain the Differences Replication Standard explain-differences Create a Panel, from a Request New Panels Strong create-panel There is no main agent: every task runs on the cell of its tier. The settings are pollis.agents.tierCells and pollis.agents.taskTiers.

Compose > Local AI Models has Get Models from Hugging Face and Get Models from Kaggle, to find and download models, and Set Active Models: the local models on this computer, those Pollis downloaded and those in the Hugging Face cache, with their Kind (Chat or Embedding), what each Reads, whether it can call Tools, and the tiers that use it. Pollis runs them with llama.cpp, which comes with it, free and private: a task on a local tier starts the model first. Evaluate Answering Models... and Evaluate Embedding Models... compare them for Ask Pollis (page ). Active AI Models, at the right of the status bar, shows the models of Pollis AI+ at a glance: of its three bars, answering at the top, reranking in the middle and embedding at the bottom, each is filled when that model is ready and outlined when it is not, and a cloud follows them while a cloud model answers. Its hover names the three models, and those not downloaded yet; a click opens Set Active Models.

Compose > Orchestration > Many Analysts... gives the same question and the same data to several coding agents, each of which answers it on its own, in a folder of its own. In Question and Data, set the data, LaLonde's job training data or a file of your own, the Question, and the Estimate to Report, which every analyst must give in the same unit. In Analysts, choose from 3 to 12 analysts, each an agent on a model: different models give a fairer spread. Start the Analysts starts them all at once, unattended. Once they are done, Check and Collect runs each analysis again in the Julia REPL, and Results shows the estimates in order, their spread, the nonstandard error beside the median standard error, and each analyst's choices.

Compose > Orchestration > Specification Curve... runs every defensible way of answering a question on the same data. Question and Data is set as in Many Analysts. In The Choices, from 2 to 4 agents each list, on their own, the decisions an analyst faces and the options of each (Ask the Agents); or Take the Study's Choices takes the samples, controls and estimators of the analysts of a Many Analysts study. Untick the options you would not defend: each specification is one option of each decision, up to 2 000. In The Code, Write the Code has one agent write , which gives each specification's rows and its estimate, and check it on every specification. Run Every Specification, in The Curve, runs them all in the Julia REPL and draws the estimates in order, the options of each beneath them, and Which Choices Matter. Run the Test, in Inference Under the Null, resamples data with the effect taken out, and gives the p-values of the curve's median estimate, its share of significant estimates and Stouffer's Z.

Compose > Orchestration > Agents' Forecasting Competition... gives the same series of M1, M3 or M4 to several coding agents, each of which writes its own forecasting method. In Competition, choose the competition, a frequency and a number of series, or 0 for all of them; Prepare the Series writes the values the forecasters saw into the study, never the values held back. In Agents, choose from 2 to 8 agents; Start the Agents starts them all at once, and each writes , a function . Score the Methods runs every method in the Julia REPL and ranks them by sMAPE, MASE and OWA, beside the mean and the median of the agents' forecasts and the competition's benchmarks; on all the series of a frequency of M4, also among the entries. An agent works on your files A coding agent reads and writes files, and runs commands, in its terminal. Read what it proposes, and check its results, as you would a colleague's. … runs on the … tier, which is in no cell & Type the tier's name in a cell of Model Tasks and Routing, or choose another tier for the task. The … tier runs the coding agent …, which was not found & Install it (Open Install Page), or put the tier in another agent's column. Not available yet Referee Report... and Systematic Review... are in Orchestration but not built yet.

Finding the articles that matter on a topic, bringing in references of your own, and following citations from a few works you know. Literature Radar asks two free, open indexes of scholarly works, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar, and keeps what you choose in PollisReferences (Pollis Databases, page ). It has four pages: Discover Literature..., Import References..., Browse References... and the Snowball Search Map.

Under Indexes, tick OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar or both. Each lists its 200 most cited articles; with both, the two lists are merged into one. Type a Topic, and choose Search In (Title and Abstract, or Title), a Field, the Years, Citations At Least and Recent Citations In the Last N Years. To keep only the best, choose an Influence percentile, a Journal Ranking (2-year mean citedness, the Norwegian levels, or SJR quartiles once imported), or Only Articles Anyone Can Read. Click Search. The table shows the citations Since Publishing and in the Last N Years, Influential citations, FWCI and Percentile; versions of one article are shown once, with +N versions. Click a title for its Abstract. Tick articles, then act on them: Save to PollisReferences, Copy BibTeX, Open PDFs, Show in Panel..., See in References, or Snowball Search..., which makes them the seeds of a map. Reconcile Sources asks each index for the counts of the articles only the other found. Keys are optional and free Without a key, OpenAlex gives everyone on your network about 100 searches a day between them, and Semantic Scholar asks searches to wait at busy times. A key of your own has its own budget or rate. Click Get a Free Key, then Set Key...; Pollis keeps it in the system's keychain.

Bring references you already have: Paste them, or choose Files and Choose Files.... BibTeX, BibLaTeX, RIS, CSL-JSON and lists of DOIs are read; the format is told by the text itself. Tick Look Up in OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar for their citation counts and the fields your file lacks (by DOI, else by title), then Import. The Tick links (All, None, Found, Not Found, Not Looked Up, Not Yet Saved) choose what Look Up Ticked, Remove Unticked... and Save to PollisReferences work on.

Browse References... lists everything in PollisReferences: the works Pollis cites, those you saved and those you imported, with the same actions. It is where a Snowball Search Map finds its seeds when you type in Add Seeds.
From a few works you know, follow the works citing them, a step at a time, until the steps bring little new. The map has two pages of its own (Snowball Search Map, page ).

Discover Literature lists the most cited, which favours older work. Sort by Last N Years or FWCI (citations against works of the same field and year) for recent work that already stands out, and use Percentile to compare fields. Influential counts the citations Semantic Scholar finds weighed on the work, not only mentioned. The free budget of OpenAlex … is used up for today & Try again tomorrow, or set a free key of your own. OpenAlex could not be reached, or refused the search & Check the connection, and try again. Semantic Scholar could not be reached, or is too busy just now & Search again a little later, with OpenAlex alone, or with a key. … has no record of this work & The other index may have it: look up its DOI there. Not found in OpenAlex (Import) & Its title or first author differs from OpenAlex's: correct the file, or keep it as it is.

Following citations from a few works you know, a step at a time, and telling when to stop. A keyword search finds what uses your words. A snowball search finds what a literature actually builds on: start from a few works you know are central, the seeds, list the works citing them, make the best of those seeds in turn, and go on. Works cited by several seeds rise to the top, whatever words they use. Pollis follows citations forward, to the works citing each seed, and backward, to the works each seed cites, from OpenAlex.

A dashed box is where seeds came from: Discover Literature, or PollisReferences for those found in Add Seeds. A pill is a seed, filled when chosen: E1 Jia (2019) is the first seed, by Jia, of 2019. Seeds are numbered E1, E2… in the order they were added. A box with ≡ is a list: L1 120 is the first list, the 120 works OpenAlex has citing E1 (up to the 2,000 most cited). Click it to see only its works in the pool. Select arrows show where a seed was chosen from; Cited by, Cites and Related arrows, the list a seed gave. Above, E3 was chosen from the pool, where it appears in both L1 and L2: it cites both seeds. Under the map, Layout: Landscape grows the map to the right, and Portrait grows it down, which shows more of a long search at once.

Every list pours into one Pool, each work once, ranked by Links, the number of seeds it cites or is cited by, then by Cited. A work that cites three of your seeds is more likely about your question than one that cites one, however cited. From names the lists a work is in, Show narrows the pool to All, one list, New Since Last Step, or Candidates, the works of the top 20 neither seeds nor excluded; Seed beside a work makes it a seed. Click Links, Year or Cited to sort by it, largest first; click again for smallest first. Sorted by Links, works tied on seeds come in order of their influential citations, the filled dots. Related lists, for each seed, the works Semantic Scholar recommends by the likeness of their titles and abstracts, mostly recent, up to 500; for a seed it has no record of, often an older one, the ten or so OpenAlex relates to it. They join the pool marked ≈, but a recommendation is not a citation: Links does not count them.

Add two to five seeds you trust: too few and the pool follows one author's network; too many and every step costs many requests. Click Cited By, for the works citing each seed, or Cites, for the works each seed cites. Each seed not followed so yet gives a list; a seed already followed is skipped. Read the top of the pool, and make seeds of the works that belong to your question, especially recent ones with several Links. Click Cited By or Cites again, and repeat. Clicking a seed on the map, or its E number in Seeds, chooses it: it is drawn filled, a note under the map names the seeds chosen, and Cited By, Cites and Related follow those alone. Click a chosen seed again to drop it, or All Seeds to follow all seeds again. The beside a seed removes it: it and its lists stay on the map, dashed, and Links no longer counts it.

The line above the pool reads, for instance, 286 works from L1–L2 · the last step added 166, 9 of them in the top 20. While a step still brings works into the top 20, the literature is still opening up. When a step adds few or none there, the search has converged: the central works are in the pool, and further steps bring only the periphery. The search goes in rounds: a round is the works made seeds, and the Cited By or Cites lists that follow them. After each round, the line below it compares the pool's top 20 with the round's before, for instance Round 3 (L5–L6, from E4, E5): 4 works new to the top 20, and marks those works ↑ New in the top 20. Make the best of them seeds and follow them. When a round brings nothing new into the top 20, the line reads The search has saturated: the stopping point the guidelines for systematic reviews call saturation. Related lists change no work's Links, so they count in no round. Run to Saturation runs the rounds for you. It follows the seeds not followed yet; then, each round, it makes the best candidates seeds and follows them, until a round brings nothing new into the top 20. Beside it, Seeds a round (5 unless you change it) sets how many candidates a round makes seeds, Rounds at most (6 unless you change it) when to stop if the search has not saturated, and Following whether by Cited By, Cites or both. Pollis remembers what you set. Stop ends the run once its round ends. The top ranks works by how central they are, not by whether they are on your question: Exclude beside a work keeps it out of the top, and so out of the candidates, and Include ranks it again.

Tick Ask Semantic Scholar About the Citations before Cited By or Cites. Each dot under Links is then a seed the work cites, or is cited by: filled when Semantic Scholar finds the citation influential, hollow otherwise. Click the dots for, seed by seed, why one cites the other (Background, Method or Result) and the sentences citing it. A work cited only in passing in the introduction is rarely a good seed; one that uses a seed's Method often is. No Semantic Scholar record leaves the ranking as it is.

Each step is kept in the map's record. Save... writes it to ~/.pollis/literature: a TOML file of the name you give, with the seeds and steps, and a DuckDB file beside it with the works found. Open... brings a saved map back; New Search starts again. OpenAlex has no record of E1 that Pollis could find & Its title or first author differ from OpenAlex's: add it from PollisReferences with its DOI. The works citing E1 are L1 already & Each seed is followed once: choose another seed, or make new ones. The free budget of OpenAlex … is used up for today & Try again tomorrow, or set a key in Discover Literature. Semantic Scholar could not be reached, or is too busy just now & Click the dots again later.

The databases of Pollis, built in and of its activity: what each holds, and how to add journal metrics. The Databases view has three groups of databases. Pollis Built-In are the databases that come with Pollis: it makes them the first time the Julia REPL starts (Getting Started, page ) and rebuilds them when what they come from changes, such as a new version of a data package, so they can always be made again. Pollis Activity are those Pollis records as you work: the items of your feeds and the runs of the Evaluate and Benchmark pages. They cannot be made again, so they are the ones to back up. User are your own. The databases of Pollis, of both groups, are read-only for you, in ~/.pollis/databases, and PollisDocuments in ~/.pollis/documents; your own tables go in a database of your own. Clicking one connects it in the Julia REPL; the duckdb> terminal, the Pollis REPL and PollisDB.connect() attach them all (Data and Databases, page ). Database In Julia What it holds PollisDatasets pollis The 69 datasets of PollisDatasets, a table each, with their descriptions. PollisJournals journals About 250,000 journals, conferences and book series, from OpenAlex; the Norwegian register's levels; and the journal metrics you import. PollisReferences references Every work Pollis cites, and those you save from Literature Radar (page ) or add to a panel's Explore References, with abstracts, keywords and dated citation counts. PollisBenchmarks benchmarks The published benchmarks of Pollis: their catalogue, with their sources, revisions and licences, and the questions of those built in. PollisDocuments documents The passages of Pollis's documents, the panel wikis, the package vignettes and the toolbox vignettes, with their embeddings, that Ask Pollis searches (page ). PollisRSS rss Every item of the feeds you follow, kept by month; empty until feeds are read (RSS Feeds, page ). Comparisons comparisons Every run of the Evaluate and Benchmark pages, with each question, answer, rating and score; empty until a page first opens.

items One row per item: feed, topic, title, link, published, received, summary, picture and media. feeds One row per feed, with its topic and number of items. zotero The items added to Zotero, with the collection. episodes The podcast episodes downloaded, with the file.

journals One row per journal, conference or book series in OpenAlex: title, ISSNs, publisher, country, field, works, citations, 2-year mean citedness, h-index, open access and article charges. journal_years The works and citations of each journal, by year. journal_issns Every ISSN, print and electronic, with its journal's id. norwegian_register The 40,000 journals and series of the Norwegian register, with field, DOAJ and the journal_id of the journal in journals. norwegian_levels Their level each year since 2004: 0 not academic, 1 academic, 2 leading, X under review. metrics The journal metrics you import (below): title, category, ISSNs, year, source, then the metrics. journal_metrics The same, with the journal_id of the journal in journals, found by ISSN. articles The articles of email alerts and those saved from Literature Radar, with journal, citations, FWCI and percentile. OpenAlex's data are CC0, free for any use. The Norwegian register is under the Norwegian Licence for Open Government Data (NLOD) 2.0, distributed by HK-dir. PollisJournals.jl brings a new copy of both every month, and Pollis rebuilds the database when it is installed. metrics, journal_metrics and articles are views over your own files in ~/.pollis/journals: always current, and never replaced by an update.

all_references Every work once, with its key (Appendix: Reference Keys), type, authors, venue, DOI, abstract and keywords; origin is pollis, corrected (yours, over Pollis's) or user. all_counts Citation counts, each with its source and the date it was observed, never added up. all_versions The records of a work you saved in OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar: the article, a preprint, a working paper. user_panels The works you added to, or hid from, a panel's Explore References. Pollis's own (pollis_references, pollis_counts) come from PollisReferences.jl and are replaced at each update. Yours (user_references, user_counts, user_versions) are views over your files in knowledge_base/references of your Pollis Workspace, never replaced: those of the workspace last opened, as a window that opens one makes the database read its folder. A work Pollis already has is not added again: it keeps Pollis's key, and only its versions and counts are yours. A work you save or correct is written in the workspace of the window, and a window without one asks you to open one. Your references kept in ~/.pollis/references before are moved into the workspace when you agree.

catalogue One row per benchmark: what it measures, its sources and the revision of each, its licence, its size in MB, how an answer is graded, whether it is built in or to download, the page that runs it and its reference. mmlu_pro, gsm8k, truthfulqa, bbh, ifeval, multipl_e_julia, pubmedqa, finqa The questions of each benchmark: id, split, stratum, question, options, right answer and worked answer, and the columns of its own, such as the unit tests of MultiPL-E or the abstract of PubMedQA. The split is test for the questions of the benchmark and example for the solved questions a prompt can show before a question. scifact, scidocs The queries and documents of each retrieval benchmark: id, split, title, text and, for a query, the ids of the documents relevant to it. The split is test for a query and document for a document. The questions come from PollisBenchmarks.jl, each at the fixed revision of its sources and under its own licence; Pollis rebuilds the database when the package is updated. The benchmarks to download are listed in the catalogue, but their questions are not in the database, by their licence or their size: a page that runs them fetches them from their source. Benchmark Answering Models runs the benchmarks of questions: MMLU-Pro, ARC-Challenge, GPQA, GSM8K, TruthfulQA, BIG-Bench Hard, IFEval, MultiPL-E Julia, PubMedQA and FinQA. ARC-Challenge and GPQA are downloaded from Hugging Face when made ready; GPQA needs your Hugging Face token, set on the page, once you have accepted its terms on its Hugging Face page. Benchmark Embedding and Reranking Models runs the retrieval benchmarks, SciFact and SCIDOCS. A published set says how a model does in general, not on Pollis's documents, so choosing the model for Ask Pollis stays on the Evaluate pages.

runs, questions, answers, scores, unrated Evaluate Answering Models: each run, its questions, each answer with its timings, each judge's ratings, and the answers a judge did not rate. embeddingRuns, embeddingQuestions, embeddingFound Evaluate Embedding Models, and Benchmark Embedding and Reranking Models for its embedding models: each run, its questions, and what each model found for each, with nDCG@10 and Recall@10 for a benchmark. rerankRuns, rerankQuestions, rerankFound Evaluate Reranking Models, and Benchmark Embedding and Reranking Models for its rerankers, in the same way. benchmarkRuns, benchmarkModels, benchmarkAnswers Benchmark Answering Models: each run with its sample and settings, each model with its figures, and each answer with its grade and timings. Pollis writes the runs to ~/.pollis/ask/Comparisons.duckdb and copies it to ~/.pollis/databases after each change: the Databases view connects the copy, so that reading it never keeps a page from saving a run. A connection shows the runs as they were when it was made; connect again for those made since.

Impact factors, quartiles and ratings are not free to share, so PollisJournals does not come with them: you bring your own, downloaded from their source, and Pollis adds them to the database. The Journal Metrics page (Explore > RSS > Journal Metrics, or right-click PollisJournals) has a card per source, with its download page, what you have imported and Remove; Ask an Agent starts your coding agent on the Journal Metrics skill, to help you choose, download and import. Source Metrics Where to get it SCImago Journal Rank SJR, its quartile, h-index Free: scimagojr.com, Download data, a year at a time CWTS Journal Indicators SNIP, IPP Free: journalindicators.com, one file with every year ABDC Journal Quality List A*, A, B, C (business and economics) Free: abdc.edu.au, the Excel file of the latest list Scopus CiteScore, its quartile Free with an Elsevier account: scopus.com/sources Journal Citation Reports JIF, 5-year JIF, JIF quartile, JCI With a Clarivate subscription, often through a university library Download the file, as CSV or Excel. On the Journal Metrics page, Import File...; or right-click PollisJournals and choose Import Journal Metrics.... Choose the file. Pollis tells the source by the file's columns, so you do not have to. The year comes from a column of the file, its headers or its name; when none has it, Pollis asks. Refresh PollisJournals: the rows are in metrics and journal_metrics. Each file imported becomes a file of Pollis's own in ~/.pollis/journals/metrics, which the two views read; the file you downloaded is no longer needed. Importing the same file again replaces its rows, and the metrics stay when Pollis or PollisJournals is updated. On the RSS Feeds page, the tags of journal items then show the SJR or Impact Factor quartile, and Journals offers SJR Q1, SJR Q1–Q2 and SNIP Above 1.

A journal's metrics from every source, newest first: SELECT year, source, sjr_quartile, snip, jif FROM journal_metrics WHERE title = 'Econometrica' ORDER BY year DESC The works you saved from Literature Radar, with their latest OpenAlex count: SELECT r.key, r.title, max_by(c.count, c.date) AS cited FROM PollisReferences.all_references r JOIN PollisReferences.all_counts c USING (key) WHERE r.origin = 'user' AND c.source = 'openalex' GROUP BY ALL Import Journal Metrics... is not in the menu & Right-click PollisJournals itself, not one of its tables, or use the Command Palette. Not a file Pollis can import & It reads the exports of the five sources above only. A file of an older edition may have other column names: Help > Report Issue. A row has no journal_id & No journal in OpenAlex has its ISSN, as for many book series and conference proceedings. Its metrics are still in the views. A journal has two rows for a year & One per source; SCImago also lists some journals twice, under an old and a new title.

Asking about Pollis, or a toolbox you installed, in your own words, and an answer from their documents, with its sources; and choosing the model that answers. Help > Ask Pollis answers questions about Pollis from its own documents, with a model on your computer. It does not search the internet, and it does not answer from what a model happens to know: every statement comes from a passage of a document, and you can open that passage.

Choose Help > Ask Pollis, or press Ctrl+Cmd+I on macOS and Ctrl+Alt+I on Windows and Linux. The first time, Pollis downloads two models, 3 GB in all, and reads its documents, in the background, for a few minutes; you can go on working meanwhile. Type a question in your own words, such as How do I make a cheap model do the small jobs?, in English or in another language, and press Enter. The answer comes in the language of the question. After each statement, a number such as [1] names its source. Under Sources, each source has its document and section, and Open shows the passage in its document: a PDF at its page, in the PDF Viewer. Ask a follow-up, such as and for Codex?: it is read with the conversation so far. New Chat, beside the title, starts again. When the documents do not answer, Ask Pollis says so, and lists the passages that came closest.

The Tour, this Guide, A Tour of Pollis AI+, The Pollis AI+ Guide, the drill-downs, the panel wikis that are written (not the stubs), the vignettes of the Pollis packages, and the documents and panel wikis of the toolboxes you installed. So a question about a toolbox's panels is answered from that toolbox's own documents, with the toolbox's name beside each of its sources. A toolbox's passages come when it is installed, and go when it is removed; a new Pollis, a wiki written or a vignette compiled brings their passages up to date, in the background. The passages are found by hybrid search: BM25 keyword search and embedding-based semantic search, merged by Reciprocal Rank Fusion into the top 8 passages, all on PollisDocuments.duckdb.

Search In can also search the APIs of the packages of the panels: every function, type, method, macro and constant with its docstring, whole, with its signature, arguments, formulas and examples. So you can ask whether a method exists for something, without knowing its name. They are left out of Auto, whose questions are about Pollis, and are searched when you tick Package APIs, alone or with other sources, and under All Sources. How a package publishes its API decides how it is read; this is the strategy for the 211 packages of the panels: Published as Packages What Pollis does A Documenter site of its own 136 Reads the docstrings from the site's pages. Only JuliaHub's copy of its Documenter site 52 The same, from the copy. A Vitepress site 3 Not read yet. A site or copy without docstrings: the API in prose, or only the README 10 Not read yet: the docstrings in the package's source are next. No published site 9 Not read yet: likewise. Part of Julia 1 Already under Julia Base and Standard Library. That is about 23,400 docstrings. Pollis reads them after the other documents, in the background: of the version you have installed if the site has it, else of the stable one, and of the latest for a package you are developing. Open shows a docstring on its site, in the internal browser. They take about 120 MB, and embedding them the first time takes about 40 minutes on a recent laptop, longer without a GPU; what is done is kept if you close Pollis. Search does not wait for them. The setting pollis.ask.packageApis turns them off.

Articles are the abstracts of the works the panels cite, from PollisReferences, each with its authors, year, venue and address; a work without an abstract is left out. A question asked in a panel searches the abstracts of the works that panel cites with its own wikis. Otherwise Auto leaves them out: tick Articles in Search In, or choose All Sources, in Ask Pollis and in Evaluate Answering Models. Open shows the reference and the abstract, with the link to the work.

Compose > Knowledge for AI Models > Knowledge Base lists openly licensed texts a model can answer from: Dive into Deep Learning, Probabilistic Machine Learning: An Introduction, Algorithms for Optimization and Algorithms for Decision Making, each with its type, subject, licence, size, what is kept of it and how it is cut into passages. On downloads a text once, from PollisKnowledge.jl, and Build the Index cuts the texts switched on into passages and embeds them. Your own texts, the PDF, Markdown and text files in the knowledge_base folder of the Pollis Workspace open, are in the same table, with User as their source and the type of their folder, books, articles or reports, switched on until you switch them off. A toolbox installed can add texts too, with the toolbox as their source: the Finance Toolbox adds Lecture Notes in Empirical Asset Pricing (PhD), whose PDF On downloads from its author's repository and checks by its SHA-256. Add Your Texts... copies files of yours there, from your Downloads folder first, or downloads one from a link, a DOI or an arXiv identifier when an open copy is found, each named by the title you write, and Rename... gives a text of yours another title. The key words and subject classifications an article prints on its first page, such as AMS subject classifications. 68N15, 65Y05, are read into Key Words and Subject Classifications, and Subject names the class of the first code, Computer science (MSC 68); Pollis keeps them in knowledge_base/catalogue.toml, and a click on a cell changes them. A PDF with its LaTeX source beside it, a .tex file of the same name, has its passages from the source, its mathematics as written, so that a model reads its formulas; From a Link or DOI... downloads the source of an arXiv article with its PDF, and LaTeX Source downloads it for a PDF of yours. Search In then lists Knowledge Base, and each collection of Compose > Knowledge for AI Models > Retrieval-Augmented Generation whose index is built, after the sources of Pollis. Auto never searches them: tick them, or choose All Sources. Each is searched in its own index, with the embedding model it was built with; ticked with sources of Pollis, most of the passages come from the index nearest the question when their embedding models are the same, and from Pollis otherwise.

The model's menu, below the box on the right, chooses the model that writes the answer: under On this computer, the chat models installed on your computer, the default one unless you choose another, and the one you choose is kept for the next time; under Cloud, with your own key, Claude Haiku or Sonnet, GPT-5.4 mini or GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.8 Flash or Gemini 4 Argon. Evaluate Answering Models... is the last item. The passages are always found on your computer; a cloud model is sent the question, the conversation and the eight passages, which are Pollis' documents, or those of the Knowledge Base and of your collections when Search In ticks them, and nothing else.

The + at the start of the question adds, as a chip above it: Image, a picture, given only to a cloud model; File, a text file; Dataset, a CSV file, given as its size, its header and its first rows; and Database, a DuckDB file, given as its tables and their columns. A long text is cut, and a note says so. PDF... opens a PDF in the PDF Viewer, whose Select Area sends the text, the table or a picture of an area of a page (Data and Databases, page ). Every panel has an Ask Pollis of its own, with its +, at the right of its title; its answer comes in the Ask Pollis pane beside the panel.

A question asked at the right of a panel's title is answered in the Ask Pollis pane, beside the panel. The question is searched as you typed it, and the reranker and the answering model are given it alone, with nothing added: a question that names its subject, as What does Check a Convergence Order check?, finds it better than one that only says this panel. In the pane, a line above the question says Asked in the panel, and the questions asked there next keep the panel until Ask Without It or New Chat. Two choices below the pane's question decide how the answer is found: Search In: Auto, the collections nearest the question, or the sources you tick, the Knowledge Base and your own collections among them. Strategy: how many passages come from the panel's own wikis, the vignettes of its packages and the abstracts of the works it cites. Base takes 5 of the 8 passages from the panel. Panel Aware takes 6 of the 8 when the panel's passages are near the question and 2 when they are not, so a question on another subject is not held to the panel. With a reranker, set in Set Active Models, three times as many passages are found, and the reranker orders the panel's own passages and the others apart, each keeping the share the search gave it: a passage of another panel that answers What does this panel check? as well as the panel's own does not push them out. Compose > Knowledge for AI Models > Answering Strategies explains the strategies, and you can write your own.

Evaluate Answering Models, the last item of the model's menu and in Compose > Local AI Models, sets the models you choose against each other on the same questions, the same passages and the same instruction: local models of different sizes, say, against Claude Sonnet. The page goes in four steps: the models, the questions, Run and the results. The questions, a test set chosen in Test Set; those ticked are asked, or all when none is. Standard comes with Pollis: 100 questions, reviewed one by one, 40 on its documents, 40 on the panel wikis and 20 on the Julia Manual, each with its answer and the passage that holds it; a newer Pollis may update it, and it cannot be changed. Panel FAQ comes with Pollis too: the closed questions of the FAQ of its panels, 5 from each of 20, and of the panels of the toolboxes installed, which Learn More does not show; each is asked in its panel with its options, and an answer is right when it chooses the right option. It cannot be changed either. Save As... copies a test set under a name of yours and New Set... starts an empty one, in ~/.pollis/ask/sets, which a newer Pollis does not change; each change is saved as you make it, the ticks too. In yours, under Change This Set, Make Questions... writes as many more as you give beside it for each topic, Pollis, Julia Language, Topic Panels, Articles and Package APIs (4, 2, 4, 2 and 0 at first), each from a passage, with the default model unless you choose another; Add takes one of your own, as does Add to the Test Set... under an answer of Ask Pollis; Import... reads them from a file of RAGTools.jl; Delete Ticked removes the ticked ones. Export... writes any test set as a file of RAGTools.jl. Tick at Random ticks as many as you give, spread over the panels or topics of the set, and the ticks stay, so that later runs ask the same questions. Passages sets where the passages come from. Found in the Library: the Strategy, one of the answering strategies of Ask Pollis (Compose > Knowledge for AI Models > Answering Strategies), finds them in the documents as Ask Pollis does, which tests the search and the answer together (open library answering). The Question's Own Passage: each model is given the passage the question was made from, or the wiki of a question of the Panel FAQ, with no search, which tests the answer alone (open book answering). None: each model is given no passage and answers from what it learned in training alone (closed book answering), which shows the questions a model answers without the documents. With Found in the Library, Search In chooses where the strategy finds them, as in Ask Pollis: Auto, any of the sources ticked, the Package APIs, the Articles, the Knowledge Base and your collections among them, or All Sources. The line of a run says what it chose. Repeats asks each question more than once, to show how much the answers vary. Run answers them with each model, one local model at a time; its label says how many questions, with how many models, and its progress how much is done. Above it, a warning names the local models chosen, and the judges on this computer, that need more memory than is free now, which would answer slowly and slow down the computer. In the results, under the figures of each model, Answers lists the questions of the run, with each model's rating by the first judge, or its answer score when the run has no judge, and its seconds: a click on one shows the right answer and the answers side by side, each with its sources, seconds, answer score and ratings, or why a judge did not rate it. For the closed questions, the figures give Right Answers, the answers that chose the right option, and By Chance, the probability of as many by guessing; a click on a question shows its options, the option each model chose and, when the author wrote one, why the right option is right. Two scores need no judge. With Found in the Library, a line under the figures says for how many questions the right passage was among those found, and at what place on average. The Answer Score says how near each answer is in meaning to the right answer of the test set: the cosine similarity of the two, by the embedding model of the search, from −1 to 1. A judge, None unless you choose one in Judge, rates each answer from 1 to 5 against the right answer, from 5, the facts of the right answer and nothing that contradicts it, to 1, wrong or unrelated; it does not see the passages. A Second Judge, such as GPT-5.5 beside Claude Sonnet, helps since a judge may favour its own family. For each model you see the answer score, the mean rating of each judge, the answers not scored, and the seconds and tokens per answer, and with Repeats above 1 how much the ratings and the seconds vary. Every run is kept, to set beside a later one.

Compose > Knowledge for AI Models > Evaluate Embedding Models... compares the embedding models on your computer on the same test sets, in the same four steps. Each model embeds the passages it has not embedded yet, once ever, then searches each question as Ask Pollis would: you see how often the passage it came from is among the eight found, and where, with words and meaning and by meaning alone, the milliseconds per question and per search, the passages a second, the memory, and the size of the index. Embed and Search Too ticks the collections Auto leaves out, Articles (ticked at first) and Package APIs, which each model then embeds and searches for every question. Use for Ask Pollis, under a model, makes it the one Ask Pollis uses. Evaluate Reranking Models... does the same for the rerankers, which put the passages found in their order. Nothing leaves your computer.

Compose > Knowledge for AI Models > Benchmark Embedding and Reranking Models... runs the embedding models or the rerankers on your computer on the retrieval benchmarks of PollisBenchmarks, SciFact and SCIDOCS, as BEIR runs them, so that the results can be set beside those published: on all the queries of a benchmark, or on a random sample of them for a quicker run. Each embedding model searches the benchmark's own documents by meaning; each reranker puts in its order the 100 documents BM25 finds for each query, beside the order of BM25 itself, as No Reranker. Each query is scored by the first ten documents found, with nDCG@10 and Recall@10. A published set says how a model does in general, not on Pollis's documents, so choosing the model for Ask Pollis stays on the Evaluate pages: this page has no Use for Ask Pollis. Benchmark Answering Models, in Compose > Local AI Models, does the same for the chat models, on published sets of questions.

pollis.ask.answerWith This Computer, or the cloud model chosen in the model's menu. pollis.ask.chatModel The chat model on this computer: the default one, or the one last chosen in the model's menu. pollis.ask.embeddingModel The model that finds passages by meaning; the default embedding model unless you change it. pollis.ask.strategy The answering strategy, chosen in Strategy: Panel Aware unless you choose another. Pollis is still reading its documents & Expected the first time, and after a new Pollis or another embedding model: wait a few minutes. A toolbox's questions are not answered & Its documents are read in the background once it is installed; a toolbox without written wikis has little to read. The answer has no sources & The documents do not answer it. Ask in other words, or use the names of the menus and settings. No key for … & Add the provider's key, or answer with This Computer. Not available yet Ask Pollis and its two Evaluate pages are not in Pollis yet; they come in a coming release.

How every work cited in Pollis is kept once, and how to write its key from the work in front of you. Pollis keeps rich references: besides its title, authors and venue, each work has, wherever they can be found, its abstract, its keywords and its citation counts over time, each marked with where it came from. Every article, book, report and package referenced in Pollis, by a panel, a notebook or a method, is kept once, in PollisReferences.jl, a package of its own. Panels, notebooks and methods name a work by its key only; the pollis.bib that reports cite from, and the references a panel shows, are built from it. A correction is therefore made in one place.

A key is the authors, the year and a letter: FF1993a (Fama and French, 1993), Bre2001a (Breiman, 2001). Anyone with the work in front of them can write everything up to the year; the letter is the database's. Authors The key starts with Example One The first three letters of the surname: a capital, then lower case. A shorter surname is used whole. Bre, Bol, Wu Two to five The initial of every surname, in the order of the work, not alphabetical. FF, TL More than five The first five initials, then ... ABCDE...2019a Some not found, after looking The initials of those known, then ...; one known author keeps the three letters. Never a shortcut: five known authors are five initials. AB...1975a, Rac...2020a An organisation The capitals of its name as printed, without Inc. or Ltd.; a one-word name that is not an acronym reads like a sole author. ECB, IMF, AV, EI, Kag None U, for unknown. U2026a

Always the last word of the surname: Lopez de Prado Pra; Puigdomènech Badia B; van Gogh and Van Gogh G; El Ghaoui G. A hyphenated surname is one word, read from its start: El-Ghaoui E; Rhys-Jones R; Ben-Tal B. As the work prints it. Accents are removed (Sánchez San, Øksendal Oks), and an apostrophe keeps the first letter (O'Neill O).

The year has four digits: 1924, 2024. A forthcoming work takes the year expected; an undated one, 0000. The letter is always there: a, then b, … z, then aa, ab, …, in the order the works are added. If FF1999a and FF1999b are taken, the next work of Fama and French from 1999 is FF1999c. A key is given once and never changes, even if the work's authors or year are later corrected.

Look the work up by its DOI and its title: it may be there already, perhaps under another spelling of a name (El Ghaoui, El-Ghaoui). Write the key up to the year, from the work itself. The database adds the letter, and lists the works already under the same authors and year. A package is cited by the paper it asks to be cited by, in its CITATION.bib or CITATION.cff; when there is none, by the package itself, with the authors it names.

references One row per work: its type (article, book, inproceedings, incollection, techreport, phdthesis, misc), title, authors, year, venue, volume, pages, DOI, arXiv and OpenAlex ids, links, a free full text when there is one, the abstract and the keywords, each with its source. A row is changed only to add what is missing or to correct a mistake. counts The citations of a work as a source reported them on a day: key, count, source and date. Rows are only added, so each source's counts can be followed over time. The type of a work is stated where it is added, never guessed from its venue. Abstracts come from the DOI's record, OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar or arXiv, and a package's from its About text on GitHub. Keywords are OpenAlex's, which it assigns itself, arXiv's subject categories or a package's GitHub topics. Citation counts from OpenAlex and Crossref are added every month; Google Scholar has no interface for this, so its counts are entered by hand. The key you wrote is taken & Expected: the database gives the next letter. Check the works it lists under that key first: one may be the same work. A work is in twice & Its name was spelt two ways. Keep the older key, and correct the other's uses.

The Julia packages created for Pollis, and the fixes to other authors' packages that they accepted. The work on Pollis also goes back to Julia's open-source packages. What Pollis needed and no package did was written as a package of its own, public and with the MIT licence, which anyone can use without Pollis (Pollis Packages, page ). Bugs found in other authors' packages were fixed and the fixes sent to them as pull requests; until a fix is merged and released, Pollis installs a fork of the package with the fix.
